title: New Creation and the Healing of the Soul
question: If I am a new creation, why do I need to work on my soul? Why find and process past memories? Can’t I just renew my mind about who I am and let God heal me?
shortAnswer: You are a new creation, fully and finally, because of what happened to humanity in Christ’s death and resurrection. Soul healing doesn’t add to that or make it truer. It is the Holy Spirit unveiling the new creation in the places of your soul that don’t yet know it, and many of those places are stored in unprocessed memory. So renewing the mind and healing memories are not rivals. Memory is very often where the mind needs renewing.

pillars.text: In Christ’s death and resurrection, humanity died and rose with him. New creation is a fact, not a project (2 Corinthians 5:14–17; 1 Peter 1:3).
The Spirit progressively opens our eyes to the One already within, ‘from glory to glory’ (2 Corinthians 3:18; Galatians 1:16).
That unveiling has to reach the places where lies were learned: the memories, body and parts that don’t know they are loved (Session 15’s definition of the flesh).

centre.title: Unveiling
centre.sub: Truth received where the lie was learned
items: The Spirit takes what is mine (John 16:14)

venn.note: The critics are right about the left circle and therapy is right about the right circle. The gospel of union lives in the overlap: the same truth, received in the place where it was never felt.

lenses.title: Cosmic
lenses.text: In the prophets and in Paul, ‘new creation’ is first a cosmic event: God renewing the whole created order, not just upgrading individuals. In Revelation 21:5 God says ‘I am making all things new’, a present-tense, ongoing verb. Creation ‘groans’ and so do we, ‘waiting for the redemption of our bodies’ (Romans 8:23). New creation is real now, yet still coming.
lenses.source: N. T. Wright, Surprised by Hope

lenses.title: Christological
lenses.text: In Bruce’s framework, new creation is what happened to all humanity in Jesus. ‘One died for all, therefore all died’ (2 Corinthians 5:14), and we were ‘born again through the resurrection of Jesus Christ’ (1 Peter 1:3). It is an objective, finished, indicative fact we cannot make, break or undo. This is why Bruce says you don’t put Jesus in; you find him there.
lenses.source: Sessions 6, 21, 26; T. F. Torrance, The Mediation of Christ; C. Baxter Kruger, Jesus and the Undoing of Adam

lenses.title: Pneumatological
lenses.text: The Spirit unveils what is true. Paul did not create Christ in himself: God ‘was pleased to reveal his Son in me’. Our transformation is a present passive process, ‘being transformed from one degree of glory to another’. The Spirit ‘takes what is mine and declares it to you’. Healing is receiving, not achieving.
lenses.source: Sessions 23, 31, 48; Gordon Fee, God’s Empowering Presence; Moyer Hubbard, New Creation in Paul’s Letters and Thought

lenses.title: Embodied and historical
lenses.tag: What it does with our past
lenses.text: The risen Jesus, the firstfruits of new creation, still bears his wounds. New creation does not delete history; it transfigures it. The scars stay, but they no longer bleed. They become the place where Thomas meets God. In the same way, healing does not erase memories. It changes what they mean and how they live in the body.
lenses.source: Sessions 34, 36, 56; Henri Nouwen, The Wounded Healer

timeline.overlap: Already and not yet: where we live and heal
timeline.note: Following Paul’s ‘two ages’ (Herman Ridderbos; Gordon Fee): new creation broke in at the resurrection, but the old age has not yet ended. Believers live in the overlap, fully new in Christ while still being renewed day by day.

words.grammar: No verb in Greek: ‘if anyone in Christ: new creation!’ The old ‘passed away’ (aorist); the new ‘has come’ (perfect).
words.meaning: An exclamation about a new reality that has arrived in Christ, with v. 16 about how we now see people. It is a statement of what is, not a promise that feelings and memories change instantly.

words.grammar: Present passive: ‘our inner self is being renewed day by day’.
words.meaning: Written by the same author, one chapter earlier than 5:17. New creation and daily renewal sit side by side in Paul’s mind.

words.grammar: Present passive imperative: ‘keep being transformed’ by the renewal of the mind.
words.meaning: The key ‘renew your mind’ verse is passive, so it is something done to us, and continuous. Even this verse describes a process the Spirit carries out, not a one-time decision.

words.grammar: Ephesians 4:23 says ‘be renewed in the spirit of your mind’.
words.meaning: In Paul, nous is the whole inner way of perceiving and evaluating, not just conscious thoughts. It includes the deep assumptions we learned through experience, like ‘I am alone’ or ‘I am bad’ (Session 52).

words.grammar: James writes to ‘my beloved brothers’ about the word ‘able to save your souls’. 1 Peter 1:9 speaks of ‘obtaining (present) the salvation of your souls’.
words.meaning: Scripture speaks of the soul of believers being saved, restored and given rest. In Hebrew the nephesh includes body and emotions (Sessions 34, 56).

words.grammar: ‘Having put on (aorist) the new self, which is being renewed (present passive) in knowledge.’
words.meaning: One sentence holds both: the new self is already put on, and it is still being renewed.

words.grammar: Perfect active (‘has perfected for all time’) together with a present passive participle (‘those who are being made holy’).
words.meaning: Perhaps the clearest single verse on this question: perfected for ever, and still being made holy. Finished and unfolding are both true at once.

words.grammar: The same verb is translated ‘saved’ and ‘made well’.
words.meaning: Salvation in the Gospels is never only forgiveness. It reaches bodies, minds and relationships, in line with Bruce’s point that Jesus came to heal the factory, not only to forgive the fruit.
Bruce reads abiding as staying present with Christ in the parts of yourself you dislike, instead of climbing out of them or dissociating (Session 22). Processing memory with Jesus is abiding.

indicative.title: Paul’s grammar of grace

nodes.label: You died; life hidden in Christ
nodes.detail: Colossians 3:3: an aorist, a finished event.

nodes.label: Old self crucified with him
nodes.detail: Romans 6:6: done in Christ’s death.

nodes.label: God is working in you
nodes.detail: Philippians 2:13: the source of all change.

nodes.label: Perfected for all time
nodes.detail: Hebrews 10:14: a perfect tense.

nodes.label: Put to death what is earthly
nodes.detail: Colossians 3:5: the ‘therefore’ that follows 3:3.

nodes.label: Count yourselves dead to sin
nodes.detail: Romans 6:11: agree with what is true.

nodes.label: Work out your salvation
nodes.detail: Philippians 2:12: participation, not earning.

nodes.label: Being made holy
nodes.detail: Hebrews 10:14: the same verse, present tense.

indicative.note: Paul never says ‘you are new, so nothing needs to change’, and never says ‘change so you become new’. He says you are new, so live from it. The soul work is the right-hand column, powered entirely by the left.

memory.title: Why the past still speaks

nodes.label: An experience
nodes.detail: Everything we live through passes through the brain’s love/fear filter (Session 55).

nodes.label: Love or fear filter
nodes.detail: The amygdala assesses safety in a fraction of a second (Session 54).

nodes.label: Safe enough: filed as past
nodes.detail: The memory is processed into narrative memory. It is remembered, but it doesn’t replay.

nodes.label: Overwhelming: stays unprocessed
nodes.detail: Above a fear threshold, it is stored raw with a ‘play again’ button (Session 55).

nodes.label: Trigger plus a hidden belief
nodes.detail: Present reactions come with a learned meaning: ‘I’m alone’, ‘I’m bad’, ‘I’m not safe’ (Session 52).

nodes.label: Truth declared in the head
nodes.detail: Affirmations reach conscious belief but often not the emotional learning.

nodes.label: Memory met with Christ
nodes.detail: The memory is gently re-activated while love and truth are actually experienced (John 16:14).

nodes.label: Head–heart gap
nodes.detail: ‘I know I’m loved, but I don’t feel it.’ Pressure to just believe harder can add guilt.

nodes.label: The lie loses its grip
nodes.detail: The emotional learning is updated and the memory can be filed as past. The mind is renewed at depth.

memory.note: Since about 2000, memory research (e.g. Nader, Schafe and LeDoux, 2000) has suggested that emotional memories become changeable again when they are re-activated. Clinicians such as Bruce Ecker describe a sequence: activate the old emotional learning, experience something that vividly contradicts it, and the learning updates. Christian practitioners see this as the Spirit bringing truth into the very place where the lie was learned.

gallery.name: Joseph
gallery.wound: Betrayed and sold by his brothers, falsely accused, forgotten in prison.
gallery.encounter: He names his son Manasseh, ‘God has made me forget my hardship’, yet when he faces his brothers he weeps so loudly that Egypt hears.
gallery.after: He reinterprets the memory: ‘You meant evil against me, but God meant it for good.’
gallery.lesson: Biblical ‘forgetting’ means no longer being ruled by the past. It came through feeling and facing it, not avoiding it.

gallery.name: David
gallery.encounter: ‘When I kept silent, my bones wasted away… my strength was dried up.’ He asks God for ‘truth in the inward being’.
gallery.after: Confession, which in Bruce’s reading is opening hidden places rather than buying forgiveness, brings relief to body and soul.
gallery.lesson: Scripture locates unprocessed pain in the body. In Psalm 42 David both preaches to his soul and laments, the two circles of the Venn diagram in one psalm.

gallery.name: Jeremiah
gallery.encounter: ‘Remember my affliction and my wanderings… My soul continually remembers it and is bowed down.’
gallery.after: ‘But this I call to mind, and therefore I have hope: the steadfast love of the LORD never ceases.’
gallery.lesson: Hope arrives inside the remembering, not by skipping it. Lament is a biblical way of processing memory.

gallery.name: Jesus
gallery.wound: Friendship, loss and the approaching cross.
gallery.encounter: He weeps at Lazarus’ tomb even though he is about to raise him. In Gethsemane his soul is ‘very sorrowful, even to death’.
gallery.after: He goes to the cross unafraid, staying fully human (Session 55).
gallery.lesson: Knowing the outcome did not cancel the grief. The perfectly whole human felt his emotions fully.

gallery.name: Peter
gallery.wound: Denying Jesus three times while warming himself at a charcoal fire.
gallery.encounter: The word for ‘charcoal fire’ (anthrakia) appears only twice in the New Testament: at the denial and at the breakfast where the risen Jesus asks him three times, ‘Do you love me?’
gallery.after: Peter is restored and commissioned in the same sensory setting as his failure.
gallery.lesson: The risen Christ did not tell Peter to forget. He recreated the scene of the wound and met him in it with love. This is the clearest gospel picture of a memory being healed.

gallery.name: Thomas
gallery.wound: Grief, doubt and being left out.
gallery.encounter: Jesus invites him to touch the wounds in his risen body.
gallery.lesson: The firstfruits of new creation still carries scars. New creation transfigures history rather than deleting it.

gallery.name: Paul
gallery.wound: His violent past, and being ‘utterly burdened beyond our strength… we despaired of life itself’.
gallery.encounter: He openly tells his past and his trauma as testimony, again and again.
gallery.after: ‘I received mercy… as an example.’ The past becomes a witness instead of an accuser.
gallery.lesson: The man who wrote ‘forgetting what lies behind’ kept remembering his story aloud, without shame.

gallery.name: The man at Bethesda
gallery.wound: Thirty-eight years of illness and waiting.
gallery.encounter: Jesus asks, ‘Do you want to be healed?’ and then, ‘Get up.’
gallery.after: Healed through an invitation that involved his will.
gallery.lesson: God heals, and he invites our participation. In Bruce’s words, self-responsibility is not self-fixing (Session 32).

objections.claim: “The old has gone. Dealing with the past denies the finished work.”
objections.short: The finished work is the reason we can face the past without fear. It is not a reason to avoid it.
objections.answer: Read in context, 2 Corinthians 5:17 is an exclamation about a new reality in Christ (‘new creation!’) and a new way of seeing people (v. 16). It is not a claim that memories and emotions are instantly wiped. The same letter says ‘our inner self is being renewed day by day’ (4:16) and that we ‘are being transformed’ (3:18). Bruce agrees the work is finished: we died and rose in Christ (Sessions 6, 21, 26). Processing the past adds nothing to it. It lets the Spirit unveil it in places that haven’t yet heard the news. As Session 35 puts it, Christ does not erase and restart us; he works with who we are.
objections.grant: The critic is right that we must never process the past in order to become accepted, forgiven or new. Any memory work done under the accuser’s ‘you must fix yourself’ is the dodgy gospel again (Sessions 37–41).

objections.short: Paul is talking about his religious credentials, not his wounds.
objections.answer: Philippians 3:4–8 lists what Paul once relied on: circumcision, tribe, Pharisaic zeal and law-righteousness. ‘Forgetting’ means refusing to rely on or be defined by it. The same Paul repeatedly retells his past (Acts 22, 26; Galatians 1; 1 Timothy 1:12–16) and his despair (2 Corinthians 1:8–9). In Joseph’s story, God ‘making him forget’ came through feeling and facing the hurt. Unprocessed memory isn’t forgotten; it replays (Session 55). Processing is how the past finally stops ruling.
objections.grant: Endless rehearsal of the past, without moving toward Christ and others, is unhealthy. The goal is to be free of the past, not to live in it.

objections.short: Isaiah means God’s former deliverances, especially the Exodus, not personal pain.
objections.answer: Isaiah 43:16–17 describes the Red Sea crossing. God tells exiles not to be fixated on how he acted before, because he is doing a new thing. It is not a command to suppress trauma. Scripture is full of commands to remember: ‘remember that you were a slave in Egypt’ (Deuteronomy 5:15), the Psalms of lament, Lamentations 3:19–24, and the Lord’s Supper, ‘do this in remembrance of me’. Faith remembers, but it remembers in the presence of the God who makes all things new.
objections.grant: Isaiah is right that God’s newness is greater than any past. Healing looks forward, not only backward.

objections.claim: “Just renew your mind. Declare who you are and God will heal you.”
objections.short: Yes, and memory is often where the mind needs renewing. Romans 12:2 is passive and ongoing.
objections.answer: The series agrees completely that identity truth is the foundation: ‘begin with the foundation of union, not with the darkness’ (Session 56). But the nous (mind) is more than conscious thought. It includes deep beliefs learned through experience, often before we had words, such as ‘I failed to make them love me, so I’m bad’ (Session 52). Declarations reach conscious belief. Emotional learnings stored in unprocessed memory often only update when they are re-activated and met with a contradicting experience of love. That is what Christian memory work aims at: the same truth received where the lie lives. Romans 12:2 itself is a present passive imperative, ‘keep being transformed’, which is a process the Spirit does in us.
objections.grant: This critic gets the most right. Many people really are healed simply by hearing and receiving who they are; Session 33 describes the undiluted gospel removing guilt and fear. Memory work without that foundation can become endless digging.

objections.claim: “Inner healing is just psychology and Freud dressed up as faith.”
objections.short: Scripture models facing, grieving and reinterpreting the past long before Freud.
objections.answer: Look at the biblical gallery: Joseph weeping and reinterpreting (Genesis 50:20), David’s body wasting under silence (Psalm 32:3–4), Jeremiah remembering until hope arrives, Jesus weeping, and Peter restored at a second charcoal fire. Jesus read Isaiah 61, ‘to heal the brokenhearted’, as his mission (Luke 4:18). The series grounds healing in Christology, not technique: ‘inner healing rests on the gospel rather than on magic’ (Session 18). It uses psychology as a description of how God made us, since all truth is God’s truth, while warning against anything that replaces relationship with method.
objections.grant: Some therapies do carry assumptions that conflict with the gospel, such as the self as the source of its own healing. Discernment is needed (David Powlison, Seeing with New Eyes).

objections.claim: “If you still struggle, you lack faith. Healing happened at conversion.”
objections.short: The New Testament describes ongoing transformation, and shaming people for struggling keeps them in fear.
objections.answer: ‘Being transformed from one degree of glory to another’ (2 Corinthians 3:18), ‘he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion’ (Philippians 1:6), ‘we groan… waiting for the redemption of our bodies’ (Romans 8:23). Paul carried a thorn that was not removed. Bruce describes healing as recursive, like snakes and ladders, with the Spirit mothering us at our own pace (Sessions 35, 59). Telling someone their struggle is a faith failure flips the amygdala to fear, which shuts down the very processing that brings healing (Session 54).
objections.grant: God does sometimes heal instantly, and expectant faith matters. The error is making instant healing the only valid pattern.

objections.claim: “Focusing on your past is self-absorption and a victim mentality.”
objections.short: Unhealed wounds leak onto others. Healing is for love to flow out.
objections.answer: Bruce sums up the whole series as experiencing the Father’s love so that it flows out to others (Session 43). Hebrews 12:15 warns that a ‘root of bitterness’ defiles many. Jesus says we must forgive ‘from your heart’ (Matthew 18:35), and we cannot forgive from the heart what we won’t acknowledge (Session 50). The series’ model is full responsibility: free and responsible for my own thoughts, emotions and actions, and responsible to others, not for them (Sessions 32, 57). That is the opposite of victimhood.
objections.grant: Healing can turn inward and stall. Good soul work keeps asking: is life flowing in love toward others? (Session 42)

objections.short: This is a real risk. The answer is not to dig, but to work with what surfaces and focus on meaning more than facts.
objections.answer: Memory research (e.g. Elizabeth Loftus) shows that suggestive techniques can create vivid but false memories, and the ‘recovered memory’ controversies of the 1990s did real harm. A gospel-grounded approach doesn’t hunt for hidden events. It works with what naturally surfaces as guilt drops (‘the mess was already there’, Session 33) and present triggers. It focuses on the felt meaning (‘I am alone’) rather than reconstructing details. Bruce notes that the brain ‘photoshops’ visual memories while body responses are more consistent (Session 56), another reason to stay with present felt experience rather than chase images.
objections.grant: The critic is substantially right about method. Never use leading questions or guided ‘recovery’ of memories, and work with trained, trauma-informed people for serious trauma.

objections.claim: “The Holy Spirit heals, not processes and techniques.”
objections.short: Agreed. Processing is making room for the Spirit to take what is Jesus’ and share it with us.
objections.answer: ‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit’ is a verse Bruce himself uses (Session 48). His practical core is John 16:14: ask the Spirit to take what belongs to Jesus, his comfort, his forgiveness and his communion with the Father, and share it with you in the place where you hurt. Jesus regularly invited participation: ‘Do you want to be healed?’ (John 5:6), ‘Stretch out your hand’, ‘Go, wash’. Participating is not self-fixing (Session 32).
objections.grant: Technique can replace relationship. If a method becomes the healer, it has become a ‘broken cistern’ (Session 24).

objections.claim: “Talk of ‘parts’ and ‘the flesh’ in believers denies that the old self is dead.”
objections.short: In the series, ‘flesh’ means the places that don’t yet know they are loved, not a second self competing with the new.
objections.answer: Bruce defines sarx not as the body or a rival nature but as ‘the dark structures where we do not know we are loved: accusation, fear, guilt and rejection’ (Session 15). Paul addresses believers who still have flesh to contend with (Galatians 5:16–17; 1 Peter 2:11, ‘passions of the flesh, which wage war against your soul’). Colossians 3:9–10 says the new self has been put on and ‘is being renewed’. Talk of ‘parts’ describes how pain splits us (Session 12). Christ’s answer is integration: ‘everything of Father, Son and Spirit leads to integration and oneness’ (Session 35).
objections.grant: Parts language can be over-literalised or used to avoid responsibility. It is a description of experience, not a new doctrine of the soul.

values: Union: Christ already in you, no separation
Over and gone; don’t look back
The key to understanding the self
Real, but held in Christ; transfigured, not deleted
The Spirit, sharing what is Jesus’, with our participation
Sacred, the soul (nephesh) itself; processed with Christ present
Holds both: finished fact and real process
Head–heart gap, suppression, shame for struggling
Misused as technique, or applied to severe trauma without trained help

children.label: All died in his death (2 Corinthians 5:14)
Born again through his resurrection (1 Peter 1:3)
You find him; you didn’t put him there (Session 23)
Renewed in the spirit of your mind (Ephesians 4:23)
Deep learned beliefs, not just thoughts
Confess to one another and be healed (James 5:16)
I am making all things new (Revelation 21:5)

practice.title: Processing a memory from the finished work

nodes.label: Stand on the finished work
nodes.detail: No condemnation. You are not fixing yourself to be accepted (Romans 8:1; Session 41).

nodes.label: Notice what surfaces
nodes.detail: Don’t dig. Start from a present trigger or feeling that keeps returning.

nodes.label: Feel it in the body
nodes.detail: Where is it? Name the emotion and breathe with it (Sessions 34, 56).

nodes.label: Ask what you learned
nodes.detail: ‘What did I come to believe here? I’m alone, I’m bad, I’m not safe?’

nodes.label: Invite Jesus into it
nodes.detail: ‘Jesus, you were there and you are here. Spirit, take what is yours and share it with me’ (John 16:14).

nodes.label: Receive, don’t manufacture
nodes.detail: Wait. Notice any shift in feeling, image or sense of presence. Nothing may happen, and that’s fine.

nodes.label: Grieve, forgive, release
nodes.detail: As needed: grieve the loss (Session 49) and unlock injustice (Session 50).

nodes.label: Live it and share it
nodes.detail: Tell a safe person. Expect the spiral to return deeper later (Session 59).

decision.title: Something from the past is stirring: where do I start?

nodes.label: Something from the past is stirring
nodes.detail: A trigger, a dream, a recurring feeling or reaction.

nodes.label: Overwhelming or unsafe?
nodes.detail: Flashbacks, losing time, self-harm thoughts, abuse, or current danger.

nodes.label: Yes: get trained help first
nodes.detail: A trauma-informed counsellor or doctor. Safety and stabilisation come before memory work.

nodes.label: No: what is it mostly?
nodes.detail: Name the main thread. Often several are tangled together.

nodes.label: Guilt and accusation
nodes.detail: Dethrone the inner judge first (Sessions 38–42).

nodes.label: Loss
nodes.detail: Grieve, make a montage and close soul ties (Session 49).

nodes.label: Injustice
nodes.detail: List the harm, own your part and hand it to Jesus (Session 50).

nodes.label: A lie about me
nodes.detail: Meet Christ in the memory, as in the steps above (Sessions 52–53).

guardrails: Never process the past to earn acceptance. Start from ‘it is finished’.
Don’t dig for memories or use leading questions. Work with what surfaces.
Go at the pace of the most frightened part of you. Rushing re-traumatises.
If you lose time, dissociate, or the memory involves abuse, work with a trained trauma-informed professional.
Keep your feet in the present. Notice your breath, the room and a safe person.
If nothing happens, that is not failure. Healing is recursive and the Spirit sets the pace.

items.title: On the Incarnation
items.author: Athanasius (4th century)
items.note: Humanity’s slide toward non-being is healed by the Word taking our nature. ‘He was made man that we might be made God.’

items.title: Epistle 101
items.author: Gregory of Nazianzus
items.note: The source of ‘that which was not assumed is not healed’, used throughout the series.

items.title: The Mediation of Christ
items.author: T. F. Torrance (1983)
items.note: The vicarious humanity of Christ: he believes, repents and is made whole for and as us.

items.title: Jesus and the Undoing of Adam
items.author: C. Baxter Kruger (2003)
items.note: A close companion to Bruce’s Volume 1, quoted in Session 15.

items.title: New Creation in Paul’s Letters and Thought
items.author: Moyer V. Hubbard (2002)
items.note: An academic study of the phrase, arguing it is mainly anthropological: an inner renewal by the Spirit.

items.title: Surprised by Hope
items.author: N. T. Wright (2008)
items.note: New creation as cosmic renewal that has already begun in Jesus’ resurrection.

items.title: God’s Empowering Presence
items.author: Gordon D. Fee (1994)
items.note: The Spirit and Paul’s ‘already and not yet’ eschatology.

items.title: Renovation of the Heart
items.author: Dallas Willard (2002)
items.note: Transformation of thought, feeling, body and relationships as ‘putting on the character of Christ’.

items.title: Emotionally Healthy Spirituality
items.author: Peter Scazzero (2006)
items.note: ‘It’s impossible to be spiritually mature while remaining emotionally immature.’ Includes looking back to go forward.

items.title: Anatomy of the Soul
items.author: Curt Thompson (2010)
items.note: A Christian psychiatrist on memory, attachment and being known.

items.title: Renovated
items.author: Jim Wilder (2020)
items.note: Joy, attachment and how the ‘fast track’ of the brain is transformed through relationship with God.

items.title: Outsmarting Yourself and The Immanuel Approach
items.author: Karl Lehman (2011, 2016)
items.note: A Christian psychiatrist on ‘the past invading the present’ and perceiving Jesus’ presence in painful memories.

items.title: Suffering and the Heart of God
items.author: Diane Langberg (2015)
items.note: How trauma destroys and Christ restores, by a leading Christian trauma psychologist.

items.title: The Wounded Healer
items.author: Henri Nouwen (1972)
items.note: Our wounds as a source of healing for others.

items.title: The Body Keeps the Score
items.author: Bessel van der Kolk (2014)
items.note: Cited in Session 34. Trauma held in the body and body-based therapies. Some of its claims are debated by researchers, so read critically.

items.title: Unlocking the Emotional Brain
items.author: Bruce Ecker, Robin Ticic and Laurel Hulley (2012)
items.note: Clinical use of memory reconsolidation: how emotional learnings are updated.

items.title: Mindsight
items.author: Daniel J. Siegel (2010)
items.note: Implicit and explicit memory, integration and the developing mind.

items.title: The Myth of Repressed Memory
items.author: Elizabeth Loftus and Katherine Ketcham (1994)
items.note: The essential caution about suggestion and false memories.

items.title: Spiritual Depression
items.author: D. Martyn Lloyd-Jones (1965)
items.note: ‘Talk to yourself instead of listening to yourself.’ The classic case for preaching truth to your soul.

items.title: Victory over the Darkness and The Bondage Breaker
items.author: Neil T. Anderson (1990)
items.note: An identity-in-Christ approach. Its ‘Steps to Freedom’ still include recalling painful memories in order to forgive from the heart.

items.title: Competent to Counsel
items.author: Jay E. Adams (1970)
items.note: The founding critique of psychology in Christian counselling.

items.title: Seeing with New Eyes
items.author: David Powlison (2003)
items.note: A more nuanced biblical-counselling voice: Scripture as the lens for reading psychology.

items.title: Destined to Reign
items.author: Joseph Prince (2007)
items.note: The grace and ‘right believing leads to right living’ emphasis many people mean by ‘just renew your mind’.

reflection: Where do you most easily believe you are a new creation, and where does it still feel untrue?
Is there a truth you know in your head but can’t feel? What memory might be holding the opposite belief?
Which picture helps you most: Peter at the charcoal fire, Joseph weeping, or the risen Christ’s scars? Why?
Which critic’s concern do you most need to hear, so your healing stays grounded in the finished work?

quiz.q: In the Greek of 2 Corinthians 5:17, what is unusual about ‘new creation’?
options: It is in the future tense
There is no verb: it is an exclamation
quiz.explain: ‘If anyone in Christ: new creation!’ The old passed away (aorist) and the new has come (perfect).

quiz.q: Which verse holds ‘perfected for all time’ and ‘being made holy’ together?
quiz.explain: A perfect tense (‘has perfected’) sits alongside a present passive participle (‘those being sanctified’).

options: A present passive imperative: keep being transformed
quiz.explain: It is ongoing, and it is something done to us by the Spirit.

quiz.q: In context, Philippians 3:13’s ‘forgetting what lies behind’ refers mainly to…
quiz.explain: Philippians 3:4–8 lists what Paul once relied on.

quiz.q: Why is Peter’s restoration in John 21 a picture of memory healing?
options: Jesus told him to forget the denial
It happens at a second charcoal fire, with three questions matching three denials
quiz.explain: ‘Charcoal fire’ (anthrakia) appears only in John 18:18 and 21:9.

quiz.q: In Bruce’s framework, where did new creation and being ‘born again’ happen?
options: In Jesus’ resurrection, with all humanity included
quiz.explain: 1 Peter 1:3: born again through the resurrection (Sessions 21, 26).

quiz.q: What does the risen Christ’s body suggest about our past?
quiz.explain: New creation transfigures history; it doesn’t erase it (John 20:27).

quiz.q: What do the critics of memory work get most right?
options: Never dig for memories or process the past to earn acceptance
quiz.explain: Healing must start from the finished work and avoid suggestive digging.

glossary.definition: The new reality inaugurated in Christ’s resurrection. In the series, humanity was included in it in his death and rising (2 Corinthians 5:14–17).
Paul’s overlap of the ages: new creation has begun but is not yet complete, so believers are new and are being renewed.
Paul’s pattern: a statement of what God has done (you died), followed by the call to live it (therefore put to death).
Research suggesting re-activated emotional memories become changeable again, so an old learning can be updated by a contradicting experience.
Knowing a truth consciously while an older emotional learning still feels true.
The Spirit revealing the Christ already present within, rather than adding something absent (Galatians 1:16).
